analysis.investment_thesis: Kajaria is India's dominant ceramic tile brand — the kind of consumer brand moat I genuinely respect — with near-zero debt (D/E 0.10), consistent free cash flow, and a well-run balance sheet built over four decades. However, the business has delivered only 2.7% net profit CAGR over nine years, FY2025 profits fell 30% year-on-year to 300 Cr, and the market prices this slow-growth business at 43x trailing earnings, which is far too rich for me to buy.
key_strengths: India's #1 tile brand with genuine consumer recognition and distribution moat — this is real pricing power
Nearly debt-free with D/E of 0.10 and consistent FCF positive all 5 years (average ~277 Cr/year)
Conservative, long-tenured promoter management with 47.69% stake aligning interests with shareholders
key_risks: Revenue and profit growth over 9 years is anemic — 7.5% revenue CAGR and only 2.7% earnings CAGR barely compensates for Indian inflation
FY2025 net profit of 300 Cr is a 30% drop from FY2024's 432 Cr — potential structural pressure from gas costs or competition
ROE of 11.2% is below my 15% threshold; the brand moat is real but the business model requires ongoing capital investment to maintain market share
red_flags: 43.4x P/E for a business that has compounded earnings at 2.7% per year for nine years is unjustifiable by any reasonable valuation framework
FY2025 other income turned negative (-14 Cr) and profits fell sharply — margin pressure from energy costs or pricing competition may be structural
At 4x Price/Sales with sub-15% ROE, the market is pricing in an acceleration of growth that has not historically materialized
analysis.detailed_analysis: Of the five businesses presented, Kajaria comes closest to what I look for: strong brand, low debt, cash generative, honest management. In a different pricing environment, this could be a wonderful investment. The Kajaria brand genuinely keeps competitors at bay — homeowners ask for Kajaria tiles by name, and that matters. But a wonderful business at an unreasonable price is still a poor investment. At 43x earnings for a business that has grown profits at 2.7% annually over nine years, I need to see either a dramatic reacceleration of growth or a significant price correction before I act.
